message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Key Points | |------|------------------------|------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Deposit may not exceed **$1,000** for a single unit or **$2,000** for a multi‑unit building.
• Landlord must return the deposit within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Deductions must be itemized and supported by receipts.
• If the landlord fails to return the deposit, you can sue for the full amount plus damages. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity). | • Texas Property Code §92.001–92.006 requires landlords to maintain essential services. | | **Lease Terms** | • Any written lease is enforceable.
• If the lease is silent on a term, the default state law applies. | • Texas law does not require a minimum lease length; however, a lease can specify a fixed term or month‑to‑month. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord can raise rent with **30 days’ notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent cannot be increased until the lease expires unless both parties agree. | • No “rent‑control” laws in Texas. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** for non‑payment of rent.
• For other reasons (lease violation, property damage, etc.), a **60‑day notice** is required.
• After notice, the landlord files an **eviction lawsuit** (forcible detainer) in court. | • You have the right to contest the eviction in court.
• If you pay the overdue rent within the notice period, the eviction may be halted. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without proper notice (usually 24 hours) except in emergencies. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • The federal Fair Housing Act also applies. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but only if you follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time to fix, etc.). | • This is a last resort; always try to notify the landlord first. | | **Right to Access Records** | • You can request copies of the lease, security deposit receipts, and any maintenance records. | • Landlords must provide these upon reasonable request. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • If your lease allows subletting, you can do so with the landlord’s written consent. | • If the lease prohibits it, you must obtain permission or risk breach. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can file a claim in small‑claims court for damages up to $20,000.
• You can seek injunctive relief (court order) to compel repairs or stop unlawful eviction. | • Consider consulting a tenant‑rights attorney for complex disputes. | --- #### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand all clauses, especially those about rent, deposits, and termination. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and photos of any maintenance issues. 3. **Give Written Notice** – If you need to terminate a lease or report a problem, send a written notice via certified mail or email with read receipt. 4. **Know the Timeline** – Pay attention to the 30‑day or 60‑day notice periods for rent increases or evictions. 5. **Seek Legal Aid** – If you face eviction or a dispute, contact a local tenant‑rights organization or a lawyer. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on landlord‑tenant disputes, how to file complaints. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Guidance on fair housing, tenant rights. | | **Local Legal Aid Societies** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance for tenants. | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Process for filing claims up to $20,000. | | **National Tenant Rights Organization** | National perspective and advocacy. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have clear statutory protections regarding deposits, habitability, notice requirements, and anti‑discrimination. If your landlord violates these rights, you can pursue remedies through the courts or state agencies. Always keep documentation and consider seeking legal advice if you encounter serious issues.
